#8708. The GLP Coaching Institute Certification: Frequently Asked Questions

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification is a comprehensive professional education program developed by Dr. John Berardi and the GLP Coaching Institute in partnership with Precision Nutrition. It combines GLP-1 science with evidence-based behaviour-change methods and practical coaching skills to help health, fitness, nutrition, and medical professionals better support clients using GLP-1 medications.

GLP-1 medications are changing the way clients eat, exercise, and recover. And many professionals are facing questions their existing education hasn’t fully prepared them to answer.

This certification helps close that gap, with specialized training in GLP-1 physiology, nutrition, exercise, recovery, and coaching. From navigating reduced appetite and protecting strength to supporting long-term maintenance, you’ll use the Five GLP Types to decide where to start and learn how to adapt your approach to the person in front of you.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification is a comprehensive professional education program that prepares health, fitness, and medical professionals to support clients using GLP-1 medications.

Developed by Dr. John Berardi and the GLP Coaching Institute in partnership with Precision Nutrition, the certification combines GLP-1 science, evidence-based behavior-change methods, and practical coaching skills in one complete program.

Across four units and 30 chapters, you’ll learn how GLP-1 medications affect the body, how to adapt nutrition, exercise, and recovery strategies to your clients’ changing needs, and how to apply a structured coaching process throughout treatment.

You’ll also develop the professional skills to work effectively alongside a client’s medical team and build a GLP-1 coaching practice.

Upon successful completion, you’ll earn the Certified GLP Coaching Specialist (CGCS) credential.

GLP-1 medications change how the body regulates appetite, weight, and energy. That means the nutrition, exercise, and recovery strategies professionals typically use may need to change, too.

For example, a client with a dramatically reduced appetite may struggle to get enough protein and essential nutrients. Someone who’s losing weight quickly may also be losing strength or struggling to recover from workouts that used to feel manageable.

Others may experience medication-related side effects, changes in their relationship with food, or plateaus that require a different approach.

Effective GLP-1 coaching means understanding these physiological changes and knowing how to adapt your support accordingly.

It also means recognizing when a client’s needs go beyond coaching and require input from their prescriber or another healthcare professional.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification was developed by Dr. John Berardi and the GLP Coaching Institute, in partnership with Precision Nutrition.

Dr. Berardi is the co-founder of Precision Nutrition and founder of the GLP Coaching Institute. He holds a PhD in exercise physiology and nutritional biochemistry and is a Certified Strength and Conditioning Specialist (CSCS). With more than 30 years of experience as a scientist, educator, and coach, he’s helped shape nutrition and health coaching education worldwide.

The GLP Coaching Institute brings specialized expertise in supporting people using GLP-1 medications, including the Five GLP Types framework.

Precision Nutrition contributes more than 20 years of experience in coaching education, behavior change, and its proven coaching methodology, which has helped train and support more than 350,000 clients, coaches, and clinicians worldwide.

Together, they’ve created a standalone professional certification that combines GLP-1 science with practical, evidence-based coaching education.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification goes beyond teaching you how GLP-1 medications work. It teaches you how to turn that knowledge into effective, individualized coaching.

The curriculum combines in-depth GLP-1 science with Precision Nutrition’s established coaching methodology and practical strategies designed specifically for people using these medications.

You’ll learn how to assess clients, identify their most pressing needs using the Five GLP Types, prioritize interventions, and adjust your approach as their circumstances change.

You’ll also work through real-world client cases and practical activities that help you apply what you’re learning, from building nutrition and exercise plans to navigating plateaus, supporting long-term maintenance, and collaborating with healthcare providers.

And because coaching doesn’t stop at the client session, the certification also covers how to develop your GLP-1 coaching services, build professional referral relationships, and communicate your expertise responsibly.

Yes. The GLP Coaching Institute Certification is grounded in current scientific research and evidence-based behavior-change principles, combined with practical coaching frameworks developed through years of professional experience.

The curriculum draws on research in obesity, weight regulation, GLP-1 pharmacology, nutrition, exercise, recovery, and behavior change.

Throughout the program, you’ll learn what the research supports, where evidence is still emerging, and how to evaluate new claims in a rapidly changing field.

The certification also incorporates Precision Nutrition’s established coaching methodology and the Five GLP Types, a framework for identifying and prioritizing individual coaching needs.

These are practitioner frameworks informed by science and coaching experience, not medical diagnostic tools or interventions independently validated through clinical trials.

The goal is to help you make informed coaching decisions, communicate accurately with clients, and recognize when questions or concerns require medical expertise.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification is designed for health, fitness, nutrition, and medical professionals who work with, or want to work with, people using GLP-1 medications.

That includes health and nutrition coaches, personal trainers, strength coaches, registered dietitians, physicians, nurses, and other allied health professionals.

You don’t need a clinical background to enroll. The certification teaches the science of GLP-1 medications in accessible language, then shows you how to apply that knowledge within your professional role.

Whether you’re working in a gym, private coaching practice, or healthcare setting, you’ll learn how to better support GLP-1 clients and collaborate with their medical team.

The certification does not expand your existing professional scope of practice.

Yes. You don’t need to be working with GLP-1 clients to benefit from the certification.

GLP-1 medications are becoming increasingly common, and more health and fitness professionals are encountering clients who use them.

In our 2026 survey of 2,490 health and fitness professionals, 65.1% reported already working with GLP-1 clients, compared with 45.8% in our 2024 survey.

This certification helps you prepare for the questions these clients may bring, from navigating reduced appetite and maintaining muscle to adapting workouts and supporting long-term health.

You’ll develop the knowledge and practical skills to work with this population before those questions arise in your own practice.

If you’re already working with GLP-1 clients, the certification will help you build on your existing skills with GLP-specific science, tools, and coaching strategies.

You may already be helping clients adjust their nutrition, maintain strength, or manage changes in energy and recovery. But GLP-1 treatment introduces challenges that traditional coaching education doesn’t always address.

You’ll deepen your understanding of the physiology behind those challenges and learn a structured approach to assessing clients, identifying priorities, adapting interventions, and measuring progress.

Through practical activities and client case studies, you’ll have opportunities to apply what you’re learning to real-world situations, including complex cases where several challenges need attention at once.

The result is a more informed, systematic approach to supporting GLP-1 clients, rather than having to figure out each new situation as it comes.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification provides comprehensive training in GLP-1 science, nutrition, exercise, recovery, behavior change, and professional coaching. Across four units and 30 chapters, you’ll learn how GLP-1 medications affect the body and how to adapt your coaching to the specific needs of clients using them.

Throughout the certification, you’ll work with practical activities, coaching tools, and client case studies designed to help you apply your learning.

The Five GLP Types are a coaching assessment and prioritization framework developed by Dr. John Berardi to help professionals identify a GLP-1 client’s most pressing challenges and decide where to focus first.

Each Type represents a different area where a client may need additional support.

Clients may experience challenges across several Types, and their priorities can change over time.

The framework helps you identify where to start, choose appropriate coaching strategies, and adjust your approach as your client’s needs change.

The Five GLP Types are not medical diagnoses. They’re practical tools for organizing coaching decisions, used alongside Precision Nutrition’s established coaching methodology.

After completing the GLP Coaching Institute Certification, you’ll have the knowledge, tools, and practical skills to assess GLP-1 clients, develop individualized coaching strategies, and adapt your approach as their needs change throughout treatment.

You’ll practice these skills through client case studies and a culminating project that brings the full coaching process together.

The goal isn’t simply to know more about GLP-1 medications. It’s to develop the practical judgment to apply that knowledge to the clients and situations you’ll encounter in your work.

Yes. The certification includes in-depth education on how GLP-1 medications work, how different medications affect the body, common side effects, and the physiological changes that can occur during treatment.

You’ll learn how to recognize medication-related challenges that affect nutrition, exercise, and recovery, and how to adapt your coaching appropriately.

However, this is a coaching certification, not a license to prescribe or manage GLP-1 medications.

Medication decisions, including starting, stopping, or adjusting treatment, remain the responsibility of the client and their prescribing healthcare professional.

Your coaching role may include helping clients meet their nutrition needs, maintain strength and function, build sustainable habits, and prepare for changes in their treatment plan.

You’ll also learn to recognize when symptoms or concerns require referral and how to collaborate effectively with a client’s medical team.

Your professional scope of practice depends on your existing qualifications and the regulations in your jurisdiction. Completing this certification does not expand that scope.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification is a standalone specialty certification focused specifically on supporting people using GLP-1 medications. It complements Precision Nutrition’s existing certifications rather than replacing them.

Each program serves a different educational purpose:

Already completed the GLP-1 chapter in PN Level 1?

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification takes that foundation much further. With approximately 80 hours of dedicated education, you’ll develop a deeper understanding of GLP-1 physiology and learn specific strategies for nutrition, exercise, recovery, and long-term maintenance.

Looking for GLP-1 coaching for yourself? This certification is designed for professionals. If you’re taking a GLP-1 medication and looking for personalized support, explore the coaching programs available through the GLP Coaching Institute.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification takes approximately 80 hours to complete and is 100% online and self-paced, so you can work through the material on your own schedule.

The certification is delivered through Precision Nutrition’s online learning platform and includes four units and 30 chapters.

You can work through the certification at a pace that fits your schedule, whether you’re balancing a full client roster, another job, or other commitments.

No. There are no prerequisites for the GLP Coaching Institute Certification, and you don’t need to have completed another Precision Nutrition certification.

The program teaches the foundational science, coaching methodology, and GLP-specific strategies you’ll need, so professionals from different health, fitness, and medical backgrounds can complete the training.

If you’re already PN-certified, you’ll recognize elements of Precision Nutrition’s coaching approach while learning how to apply them specifically to clients using GLP-1 medications.

After successfully completing the GLP Coaching Institute Certification, you’ll earn the designation Certified GLP Coaching Specialist (CGCS), issued by the GLP Coaching Institute.

This credential recognizes your completion of specialized professional education in supporting clients using GLP-1 medications.

The certification will include a renewal process to help professionals stay current as GLP-1 science and coaching practices evolve.

The GLP Coaching Institute Certification can help you expand your expertise, better support clients using GLP-1 medications, and develop specialized coaching services in a growing area of health and fitness.

#8707. Reviewed: The EZ Hydro-Glide Swim Cap

Jumping into frigid water is nobody’s idea of fun – unless you enjoy the crippling pain of ice cream headaches without the pleasure of an actual ice cream cone. At the opposite end of the spectrum, swimming in very warm water can also crater your comfort and results. That’s why we were psyched to test the EZ Hydro-Glide Cap, a one-of-a-kind attempt to boost swimming performance and safety using wearable technology designed to enhance thermoregulation.

In plain English: The Hydro-Glide is a potentially game-changing swim accessory that’s supposed to make you less susceptible to cold shock and heat stress.

Before we dive into the science, an important clarification: The critical technology here is not a cap, but a 3D-printed contraption that goes under your cap. More on that below.

But first, kudos to EZ Gains, a popular outside-the-box triathlon retailer, for attacking a problem that numerous triathletes experience – significant discomfort when swimming in very cold and very warm water. We’ve learned a lot in recent years about thermoregulation, and any improvements in this area could help many athletes, including friends of mine who’ve quit the sport after repeated unpleasant swims.

EZ Gains’ approach is based on credible science. The company notes that your head plays an outsized role in your body’s response to ambient temperatures, given the extensive network of blood vessels and nerves just beneath your scalp. This rings true, as does the contention that regulating the temperature difference between the water and your head – both the initial gap and the ongoing variance – can mitigate the downsides of extreme heat and cold.

We use insulated neoprene caps for chilly swims, after all. What if a single, more sophisticated solution helped us thrive in both polar and equatorial waters?

EZ Gains’ answer is a honeycombed high-tech foam and hard plastic wedge that sits at the top of your forehead under an (included) standard swim cap. Before putting it on, you can place one or two small thermal packs (also included) inside the hollow center of the wedge. These packs – and an additional thin heating strip – provide a cooling or warming effect as needed. In warm water, you can use a frozen pack or two to cool your forehead, which is meant to keep your core temp down and reduce heat fatigue.

You’re also supposed to use frozen packs when swimming in frigid water – say 60 degrees F or less – according to EZ Gains. The idea is to pre-condition your head to the chilly temps you’re about to encounter. This may sound counterintuitive, but EZ Gains says the pre-cooling technique can prevent cold shock, a serious autonomic response that elevates your heart rate and can cause panic and even cardiac arrest. The packs can also be heated for a touch of warmth when facing cool-but-not-arctic conditions.

For more preparation for swimming in cold water, read: How to Acclimate and Prepare for Cold-Water Triathlons

To evaluate the system, I tested it in various bodies of water over the course of five months, from midsummer to late autumn. My primary locations were indoor and outdoor pools in Boulder, Colorado, and our local reservoir. Water temperatures ranged from 84 degrees F all the way down to 50 degrees F. All of my swims were 45-90 minutes long, more than enough to mimic race conditions and assess how well the device limits heat and cold stress.

The TLDR from my testing: Some new technologies sound great on paper but don’t pan out in real life. Sadly, this device is one of those. On two of its three core value propositions, the Hydro-Glide fell short. I’ll tackle them one by one.

First, EZ Gains says the cap will reduce heat fatigue and related complications – anxiety, increased heart rate, dehydration, and confusion – when using the frozen packs. I did notice a cooling sensation in the early parts of my summer swims, typically lasting 10-15 minutes. But while I appreciated the initial cooling, I didn’t discern a material difference in fatigue, judgment, or heart rate after an hour, even during my most intense workouts.

Second, the cap is supposed to prevent the instant discomfort and cold shock that many people experience when diving into frigid water. Perhaps I’m less sensitive than other athletes (my long-suffering wife might have an opinion on this), but using slightly thawed ice packs to pre-cool my head (as instructed) didn’t eliminate the ice cream headaches.

In my experience, this kind of pain starts in my face and forehead, neither of which are protected by the device. It’s possible that the Hydro-Glide would help other swimmers, since physiological reactions vary widely, but I’d speculate that too much of your face, forehead, and neck remain exposed for the cold to be significantly neutralized.

Third, EZ Gains says the cap will protect your head when another swimmer clobbers you, which seems legit in the case of head-on impacts. A friend in my Masters group sustained a concussion last year when another swimmer swerved into her during a backstroke set. While I didn’t do any head-banging to test this claim, it’s reasonable to believe the Hydro-Glide’s foam would’ve absorbed that blow. Since the wedge doesn’t cover the sides or back of your head, though, it wouldn’t deflect all-too-common errant elbows or kicks to those areas during a race start.

There are two additional downsides to consider. If you have an XL melon like mine, you may experience discomfort from the pressure of the cone against your head. I did, typically after about 30 minutes. And if you’re even the slightest bit fashion-conscious, you will probably draw the line at looking like a Corythosaurus from Jurassic Park. The first time I showed up at the pool wearing the Hydro-Glide, several of my masters teammates burst out laughing. Someone compared me to a Conehead.

Which I could possibly live with if the results had been stellar. However, the Hydro-Glide didn’t deliver a meaningful upside for me versus a standard swim cap. While EZ Gains deserves praise for its waaay-out-of-the-box effort to improve swim safety and comfort, this product’s current execution doesn’t justify a $270 investment.

#8706. Best Cheap Exercise Bikes That Feel Surprisingly Expensive

Light on price, heavy on performance—these cheap exercise bikes deliver the best ride for your money.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

There are plenty of reasons to start riding inside. Questionable weather, overly packed schedules, and less daylight can cause outdoor riders to head inside for some indoor saddle time. It’s also possible you’re someone who doesn’t ride outside and you just want a good low-impact workout in the comfort of your own home—without breaking the bank.

Recently we did extensive testing in the office on different exercise bikes. I found that some people who don’t ride bikes outside may actually prefer some of the less expensive exercise bike options. Some of the higher-end exercise bikes we tested feel like a real bike outside—and pair with specific apps like Zwift for when you want to get some group rides or racing in. If you aren’t used to a bike outside, then getting comfortable in that position can be a hard transition. More narrow saddles, a more aggressive position, and controls that simulate the shifters on a bike may not be what you want. Largely, these more inexpensive exercise bikes have more upright positions, wider and more padded saddles, and controls that would resemble the exercise bike you might see on the floor of a fitness center.

Keep in mind that inexpensive is relative—the bikes we have on this list range from about $200 up to $700. If you’re looking to boost your mood, stay consistent, or supplement your training with an affordable indoor cycling bike, these cheap exercise bikes deliver the best mix of value, performance, and reliability.

If you're further along in your indoor training journey and none of the bikes on this list feel like the right fit, take a look at our reviews of the Peloton, Zwift Ride V2, and other premium models.

This budget-priced, belt-driven bike operates a 35-pound flywheel that provides a smooth and quiet ride. The resistance is adjustable via a knob regardless of pedaling speed. It also has an emergency brake that stops the flywheel immediately, if necessary. According to Yosuda, the seat height adjusts to fit riders with inseams from 25 to 35 inches, and allows riders to adjust the handlebar height as well as the fore-aft alignment of the padded saddle.

Using the single-button monitor, you can scroll through your time, speed, distance, and calories burned as you exercise. Just below the monitor is a platform for a phone or tablet. The heavy-duty steel frame is designed to provide stability and durability, but it's easy to move if you tip it up onto the small wheels on the front edge.

Besides being designed to look like an entry-level Peloton, the Yesoul S3’s biggest selling point is its Bluetooth connectivity, which pairs with the Yesoul Sports App (on both iOS and Android) and works with Zwift and other interactive training apps. All your workout data, including distance, time, calories burned, speed, heart rate, odometer, and cadence, is tracked and easy to access.

The bike has a quiet belt drive and magnetic resistance, with 100 levels that are easy to adjust with a knob. With a height- and distance-adjustable seat and handlebar, the S3 is built to fit riders from 4-feet-9-inches to 6-feet-2-inches—though riders at the higher end of that range and those with disproportionately longer legs might find the riding position to feel a bit “off.” The bike is easy to move on two small transport wheels, and it comes in both white and black models for a sleek, Peloton-like aesthetic.

This is a fantastic price for a budget bike that delivers a Peloton-like experience. It has the same sleek silhouette, with a saddle that adjusts both up/down and fore/aft, plus an adjustable handlebar height—just like the real thing. The belt-drive system is another big plus, keeping noise to a minimum so the only sounds you hear are your own effort (and hopefully some music to cover it up).

To keep costs down, this bike skips the large built-in display, instead offering a tablet holder and Bluetooth connectivity. That means you can ride with any third-party app you prefer—including Peloton classes—using your own device. At this price, it’s a fair trade-off. But if you want a built-in screen, Merach offers a similar model with that feature for about $450 more

Merach’s newest bike, the A26 Aura, is one of the best Peloton competitors I’ve seen. It follows the familiar design cues of premium exercise bikes — a sturdy frame, heavy flywheel, and whisper-quiet belt-drive system. The seat adjusts up and down as well as fore and aft, and the handlebar also moves vertically for a comfortable fit.

At its current sale price, the Merach A26 Aura makes a compelling case as one of the best values on this list.

The Echelon Connect Sport 2 delivers a Peloton-like experience at a more affordable price. It connects via Bluetooth to the Echelon Fit app, allowing you to track speed, distance, and calories. If you’re taking a live class, you can also view your ranking on the leaderboard. The app offers over 40 live classes daily and a library of more than 15,000 on-demand sessions. While the bike doesn’t have a built-in screen, its device holder accommodates tablets up to 8 inches wide.

That said, you don’t need the connected features to get a great workout. At its core, this is a solid, well-built exercise bike with a heavy flywheel and 32 resistance levels, manually adjusted with a knob behind the handlebar. The bike features a “one size fits most” design, with adjustable saddle and handlebar positions to suit most adults. However, some shorter riders have reported difficulty positioning the saddle close enough to the handlebars for a comfortable fit.

With Bluetooth and USB connectivity to the Schwinn ConnectTM, Zwift, and MyFitnessPal apps, this stationary bike is a great option for interactive workouts—particularly if you want to work through pre-programmed sessions and track your progress over time. The bike has the standard DualTrack console shared by similar-level Schwinn and Nautilus products, which has two sharp, backlit LCD screens loaded with 29 workouts.

Unlike many of the bikes we've selected that adjust gradually in difficulty at the turn of a knob, this model has 25 preset levels of magnetic resistance, which provides a nice range in difficulty. The seat and handlebar adjust by height and angle to fit users from 4-feet-6-inches to 6-feet-6-inches; however, as always, those at the far ends of the range might have more difficulty getting a comfortable fit. Ultimately, the bike is a solid package for the price—especially if you can catch one on sale for around $400.

Looking for a cheap home exercise bike that will neither take over your space nor break the bank? When not in use, this compact device folds down to half its size and can be easily rolled into a closet or tucked under a bed.

While it may have a minimalist design, it still has the basic functionality needed for a workout. It touts 12 levels of magnetic resistance, adjusted via a knob below the handlebar, that allows you to adjust the intensity as needed. The built-in LCD screen, although very basic, keeps track of key workout stats, including distance, time, speed, calories burned, and heart rate.

Users love how quiet this bike is, making it perfect for multitasking or watching TV while riding. Though it may not provide the high resistance some hardcore riders seek, many praise it as a “sturdy, well-built machine” with a “comfortable seat and great height adjustability.”

Just like with a regular bicycle, if you want the best experience on your indoor bike, it’s important to get the proper fit. Josh Taylor, a global brand ambassador for the online fitness site Spinning, recommends finding an indoor cycling bike that puts you in the same position as the bike you’re accustomed to riding outside.

For example, if your daily rider is a road bike, look for an indoor cycling bike with a handlebar option that incorporates a traditional bullhorn bar and mimics the hand-position options of drops and brake hoods. However, if you’re already used to taking studio classes, an indoor cycling bike with just the traditional bullhorn-style bar will work great, says Ben Sharp, three-time Order of Ikkos medal recipient and founder of Sharp Coaching.

If you don’t ride at all outside or in a spin class yet, then it will take a bit more playing around with the exercise bike to figure out sizing and position. Start with getting saddle height set up correctly, then if you can adjust reach to the handlebars that’s step two. For the reach shoot to have a slight bend in the elbows and remember to keep your shoulders relaxed and away from your ears. Matt Phillips, Senior Test Editor at Bicycling, recently published a story on dialing in saddle height. What applies to saddle height on an outdoor bike largely applies to exercise bikes as well. “A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel,” says Phillips.

Join Bicycling All Access for more in-depth gear reviews

When you’re riding an outdoor bike, you’re mostly working against inertia as you pedal. In order to recreate that sensation and effort on a stationary bike, manufacturers have to simulate that resistance in some way. Most choose to use a fan or a flywheel (a weighted disc that spins as you pedal).

Flywheels work by storing inertia as they spin, and smoothing out the pedal stroke to eliminate that choppy up and down motion you’d otherwise experience. For most budget spin bikes, a heavier flywheel means a smoother ride, though some bikes opt for a light (8-pound) flywheel that maintains its inertia by spinning four times as fast instead.

Since the pedals on spin bikes are fixed to the flywheel (no coasting), the smooth-moving mechanism helps keep your pedaling consistent. These bikes will usually have a knob or lever that allows you to adjust the resistance, making it harder or easier to pedal, independent of your cadence (how fast you’re spinning the pedals). If you’re used to riding a bike outside, then think about it like riding a fixed-gear bike or fixie.

Fan-operated resistance bikes are a bit simpler: As you pedal, the fan blades push against the air around the machine. Your cadence is directly related to the amount of effort required to push the pedals, meaning these bikes don’t allow you to spin at a fast cadence with low resistance, which can be nice for warming up or cooling down.

#8705. 3 Restorative Yoga Poses for When You’re Stressed and Short on Time

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about restorative yoga poses appeared in the September-October 1995 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

In a perfect world we would all have time for a long restorative yoga practice daily. But obligations to work, family, friends, and community often leave us with little time for self-care. It is precisely when we are the most stressed that we need to relax and renew ourselves, and bring some restorative yoga into our busy lives.

Traditionally, a yoga class or personal practice session begins with active poses followed by a brief restorative pose. However, the entire focus of this practice is on supported restorative poses.

To relax deeply in this amount of time, you must have a quiet room, but you can get by with a minimum of props. There are only three poses: Legs-Up-the-Wall Pose, Supported Child’s Pose, and Basic Relaxation Pose. Practice them in the order presented. If you can’t find even 15 minutes, practice Basic Relaxation Pose for five.

This pose is simple to practice, even when traveling. Just lie on your back and let a nearby wall support your legs. This pose brings the blood and lymph fluid to pool in the abdomen, refreshing the leg muscles and enhancing the health of the circulatory system. In addition, the pose reverses the energy of the legs from moving down and out to the feet, as in our normal stance, to moving down and back to the pelvis. Nothing feels better to tired legs and feet than being elevated.

Setting Up. To begin, sit on the floor with one shoulder near the wall and your thighs parallel to the wall. Roll back as you swing your legs up the wall. Once in position, make sure that your lower back is not rounded and your tailbone and buttocks are not lifting off the floor. If they are, move slightly away from the wall so your lower back is comfortably supported by the floor.

If your chin lifts toward the ceiling, place a standard-fold blanket under your head and neck to support your cervical curve. Make sure your chin is slightly lower than your forehead, but do not force your chin down and flatten the back of your neck.

Keep your legs straight but relaxed. Place your arms out to your sides with the palms turned up. Close your eyes. Place an eyebag over them.

Being There. Take several long, slow breaths. As you do, imagine the fluid in your legs flowing down toward the abdomen. With it, all tension drains out of your legs. They begin to feel lighter and softer. Imagine that your brain is shrinking in size as it moves away from your forehead and sinks toward the back of your head and the floor. Feel your entire spine supported by the floor. The position of the arms creates a feeling of being open and free. Enjoy this feeling.

Coming Back. Practice Legs-Up-the-Wall Pose for five minutes. When ready, remove the eyebag and open your eyes. Rest for a few breaths before bending your knees toward your chest and rolling to one side. Pause again for a few breaths before slowly coming to a sitting position with the help of your arms.

Benefits. Legs-Up-the-Wall Pose reduces swelling and fatigue in the legs.

Cautions: Do not practice this inverted pose

Supported Child’s Pose is the familiar posture of rest and sleep for babies and young children. When you practice this pose, not only will it help to relieve tension in your lower back, but it may evoke a sense of security from your earliest days. This pose is one of introversion, one of curling up and reconnecting with feelings of support and release.

Setting Up. Begin by kneeling on a carpeted floor or blanket with your knees hip-width apart and your bolster in front of you. Use more padding under your knees and shins if you need it. To avoid stress on the ligaments of your outer ankles, point your toes directly backward and not toward each other. Sit back on your heels.

If you experience discomfort in your knees, ankles, or tops of your feet, come up and try one or both of the following adjustments. Place one towel, folded lengthwise, into the bend of your knees to create more space in the knee joints. Place the other towel, rolled lengthwise, under the front of the ankles, and let your feet hang over the roll. Experiment with the thickness of these folded and rolled towels to get them just right for you.

Sit back on your heels again. Separate your knees wide enough to place the bolster between your thighs. To enhance relaxation, hold a sandbag across your lower back as you bend forward. The weight of the bag helps to relax the muscles of your lower back.

Your torso should be completely supported by the bolster and your thighs. Your chest should rest easily on the bolster. Let your tailbone drop toward your heels. This action will lengthen your lower back as you relax. Your buttocks do not have to touch your heels.

If you need more support, try one of the following variations. Come up to a kneeling position and place a long-roll blanket on your heels and sit back, or come to a kneeling position and significantly raise the height of your torso support by adding one or more single-fold blankets. If you have difficulty breathing, push the bolster forward so it only supports your breastbone and lets your belly hang free.

Turn your head to one side and bring your chin slightly toward your chest. Turn it to the opposite side halfway through the practice of Supported Child’s Pose. If the side head position is uncomfortable, rest on your forehead and slightly tuck your chin toward your chest. Make sure you can breathe easily regardless of your head position.

Place your arms so they reach either back toward your feet or forward around the edges of the bolster. The position of the arms is unimportant; it is important that you are comfortable. Close your eyes.

Being There. Take several slow breaths. As you do, let your shoulders move away from the ears. Let your belly relax and feel supported. The counter-pressure of the bolster on the belly may feel especially good if you have menstrual cramps.

Coming Back. Practice Supported Child’s Pose for three minutes. Be sure that you spend equal time with your head turned in both directions. Open your eyes. Reach back with one hand and slide the sandbag off your back and to one side. Place your palms on the floor, under your shoulders. Press your hands into the floor, inhale, and sit up slowly onto your heels. Rest for a moment. Come to a kneeling position and immediately bring one leg forward, placing your foot on the floor. Press your hands on the forward thigh, and inhale deeply as you come to a standing position. Coming out of the pose in this way prevents discomfort in the knees.

Benefits. Supported Child’s Pose gently stretches the lower back, relieves shoulder tension, and quiets the mind.

This pose is the heart of restorative practice. Relaxing completely, even if it is only for five minutes, is one of the most important skills you can acquire. When you have learned to relax whenever and wherever you need to, you can use this skill in a variety of situations to reduce stress and its accompanying fatigue.

The less time you think you have for spending a few minutes a day in Basic Relaxation Pose, the more you need to do it. If you do nothing else for your health every day, make time for this pose. Practice it, for example, at an afternoon break at work, when you first come home from work, after a workout session, or whenever you feel depleted, exhausted, or stressed.

Setting Up. In Basic Relaxation Pose you will be lying on your back with your arms out to the sides and your legs comfortably apart. Give yourself enough floor space to spread out comfortably. Before you lie down, position a standard-fold blanket for your head and neck to rest on.

Begin by sitting on the floor. If you have a tendency to get cold, cover your legs with an unfolded blanket. Now turn to one side and lean on your elbow and forearm as you slide onto your side. Then roll onto your back. Coming into the pose in this way is less stressful on your back than leaning back into a reclining position.

Roll the long edge of your standard-fold blanket slightly to support the gentle curve of the neck. Adjust the prop placement so that your neck is comfortable. Your chin should be slightly lower than your forehead. This position quiets the frontal lobes of the brain. If you are using an extra blanket for warmth, now is the time to pull it up to cover your torso and arms. Cover your eyes with an eyebag.

Many people can practice this pose lying flat on the floor. If you have tension or pain in your abdomen or lower back, place a long-roll blanket under the backs of your knees before you lie down. Make sure that your legs are relaxed and the knees supported by the long-roll blanket. If your heels do not touch the floor, place a folded blanket or pillow under them. If your lower back discomfort persists, come out of the pose by following the instructions under Coming Back (below). Resume your practice of Basic Relaxation Pose when you feel ready.

Once you have established yourself, observe the position of your body. Your arms and legs should be equidistant from an imaginary line drawn from the tip of your nose to exactly midway between the feet. Most people practice with the palms turned upwards, but if this is not comfortable, turn them down and let the elbows relax. The most important thing is that you feel completely at ease and supported by the props and the floor. If you need to sit up to adjust props and lie down again, follow the instructions for Coming Back and Setting Up.

Being There. Swallow and relax your lower jaw. Soften your upper eyelids and look down toward the lower lids as you close your eyes. Let your cheeks feel hollow and loose beneath the cheekbones. Release the root of your tongue. Your fingers will curl naturally as your hands relax. Let your legs roll outward. Allow the entire back of your body to feel at ease and in complete contact with the floor and the props.

Your arms and legs will feel longer and longer, as well as heavier. Feel the large muscles of the legs, buttocks, and trunk drop away from the bones. Now feel the smaller muscles of your arms, neck, and head as they seem to move away from the bones. Let the bones themselves feel heavy and the skin loose, all over your body. Notice that the abdominal organs seem to nestle gently back into your body. Savor the silence.

The Centering Breath. As you continue to rest, notice when you begin to feel lighter. This is a signal that your body has relaxed and that you can begin the Centering Breath: a long inhalation followed by a long exhalation, followed by several cycles of normal breathing.

Begin by slowly inviting the inhalation to move more deeply into your body. Do this by lifting your ribs slightly and spreading your lungs. Let the air come to you. As you inhale, imagine that the breath breathes you. Follow the inhalation with a soft focus on the exhalation. Feel your diaphragm, lungs, ribs, and muscles of respiration contracting to press the breath out in a steady and focused stream. When your exhalation is finished, breathe several normal cycles of inhalation and exhalation.

Then inhale slowly and deeply once again. At the fullness of inhalation, pause slightly before melting the inhalation into an equally long and steady exhalation. The inhalation is the receptive part of the breath; the exhalation is the active part. Once again, take several normal cycles of breath.

Once you have established the rhythm of the long breaths, pay particular attention to the quality of these breaths. What is their texture? Is the beginning of inhalation as soft as the end of inhalation? Is the end of exhalation as smooth as the beginning? With each cycle, allow your breath to become more and more refined, like the texture of fine silk.

Remember, never strain or force the breath. If at any time you feel even slightly agitated or out of breath, simply return to normal breathing. Once you feel calm, resume the cycle of long, slow inhalation and exhalation, followed by several normal breaths.

The success of the Centering Breath is not measured by how much air you can take in or let out. So go slowly, gently, and be present with the process. If you feel fatigued, anxious, or light-headed during practice, it is an indication that you have practiced long enough. Let your breathing return to normal, and, in the future, take longer breaks of normal breathing between each round of long inhalation and long exhalation. Do not practice the Centering Breath if you have a fever, a bad cold, sinusitis, or more serious respiratory diseases, such as pneumonia.

Repeat the Centering Breath for up to 10 rounds. Be sure to leave some time for normal breathing before coming out of the pose.

Coming Back. Remain in Basic Relaxation Pose for five to 20 minutes. To come out of the pose, bend one knee and roll onto your side. Let the eyebag fall off by itself. Gradually open your eyes. Rest in this position for a few breaths. To sit up, press the floor with the elbow of your lower arm and the palm of the hand of your upper arm. Sit quietly for several breaths before standing up and resuming your normal activities.

Benefits. Basic Relaxation Pose lowers blood pressure and heart rate, releases muscular tension, reduces fatigue, improves sleep, enhances immune response, and helps to manage chronic pain.

The author gratefully acknowledges her teacher B.K.S. Iyengar and his book Light on Yoga in the writing of this article.

#8704. The 6 Best Folding Treadmills for Runners, Tested by a Treadmill Expert

We tested folding treadmills for running feel, size, storage, portability, speed, incline, and more to find the best models for every type of runner.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The best folding treadmills give you a real running experience without permanently eating up your floor space. I adore having a folding treadmill at home, because, living in a smaller space, I can easily stash it away or bring it out for a go. And this time of year, when there's sleet and snow? I don't want to miss out on a workout.

If you're like me and you want to be able to run a treadmill at home, but you can’t give away valuable space to a huge piece of fitness equipment? We get it. There’s a solution, though: A folding treadmill gives you the ability to pack up and store your ’mill between runs. Their compact size and light weight comes at a cost: They often don’t have as many convenient features we expect from a top-of-the-line model, nor do they offer huge inclines and top speeds. That said, most can do the basics effectively when you need them to, then fit in your closet when you’re done. The best folding treadmills, as we see them, offer a range of sizes and prices for casual runners and athletes in training.

The dream of shoving your treadmill under your bed between runs is alive in the Echelon Stride-6. This high-performance mill features a full-size, 20.5- by 60-inch running deck that can hit a max speed of 12.5 mph, but still manages to fold up tight. Personally, I store mine upright against a wall, sometimes hidden behind a curtain. It takes up about as much space as a few snowboards or a couple of winter coats. No, I'm not kidding, it's just that compact.

The Stride-6’s belt features low-response cushioning that creates a ride that feels closer to outdoor road running than treadmill running, which I love when I’m training for road races. Also, as an autistic sensory seeker, sometimes I really enjoy beating the hell out of the deck after a bad day. Are you also a sensory seeker, or have one in your life? If so, this is a solid choice. At full speed, with a 12 percent incline, this machine gives as good as it gets, too.

This treadmill does not have a touchscreen, though. Instead, it syncs directly to a running watch or tablet, for which it has an extra-large holder. The pre-loaded running programs are fine and dandy, but nothing to write home about. Echelon produces a paid workout video library like NordicTrack’s iFit, which you can access via an app, but it’s no different than any other virtual workout platforms without native support on the treadmill.

Let’s talk a little more about the folding mechanism, though, because that’s the reason to buy this treadmill. It is one of only a handful of options that doesn’t require any assembly. Unbox this beauty, unfold it, plug it in, and you’re good. It has an “autofold” feature that makes collapsing the treadmill feel seamless. All that you do is press the foot pedal, and the crossbar and board fold onto the surface of the treadmill. You can then store it flat on the ground or upright, which is a win for anyone who doesn’t have the permanent floor space available.

Also, after testing treadmill after treadmill in my house, I can confidently say my cats prefer the Stride-6, and I have no idea why. They're obsessed and I can't figure it out. It is also the easiest to store, fun to run on, and it's by far the easiest to move around.

When this treadmill is folded, it practically disappears. Fully folded, it drops to under 11 inches tall, which is easily flat enough to slide under a bed or stand upright in a closet corner. For anyone training for a marathon in an apartment, a spare bedroom, or a shared space, you know the value there. The SwiftFold mechanism handles it in one motion, and there’s no assembly required.

What I appreciate is that folding this flat usually means compromising on the machine underneath. This one doesn’t. You still get a dual brushless 4.0 HP motor, a 0–12 percent auto-incline, a 12.5 mph top speed, and a 300-lb weight capacity that matches most treadmills in its class. The 51.18 x 18.9-inch deck is a touch narrow for tall runners, and that is, admittedly an issue.But, when you add the real marathon course maps and an AI coach, along with that magical fold? At around $900 to $1,000 it’s a ‘mill that’s hard to say no to.

I will be the first to admit I was incredibly skeptical about this machine. I mean, it folds up to be smaller than your average card table. I have luggage that’s bigger than the G5i. But, I hear the cawing coming because I need to eat crow. It’s surprisingly stable and fun to run on. It’s really pretty smooth. It is more road-like than cushioned, so if you’re expecting pillowy surfaces, you’ll be disappointed. But if you’re worried you’re going to feel the fold seam, or feel super penned in, you won’t.

No, this is not a treadmill for tall runners. I’m 6-feet tall, and I’m at the tippy top end of the range of someone who should throw miles on this. But, that being said, if you’re shorter than I am, starved for space, and you want a folding treadmill with serious speed and incline, this is a fantastic option. One thing I will note, though: that first fold when you’re folding it isn’t as soft as you’d expect, and it’s kinda loud. But considering the fact that you could store it just about anywhere, and that it takes less than five minutes to set up and assemble? It’s freaking impressive as all get out. Like, truly wild territory, here.

If you’re looking for a serious running machine that also happens to fold, then you can’t do better than the NordicTrack Commercial 1750. Both Dengate and I really appreciated the feel of running on this machine, which has he called “Goldilocks” cushioning. The deck is firm enough that you don’t feel like you’re running on rubber but soft enough that it wasn’t as hard on our joints as a road run would be. We were also sold on the quick controls for both speed and incline changes, which are both easy to identify and toggle. I found that it stops a bit more abruptly than other NordicTracks: It’s not “knock you off your feet” fast, but there’s a little learning curve.

The Commercial 1750 has a large running surface, which I appreciate as someone who tends to wander on the ’mill a bit. All NordicTracks come with a trial subscription to iFit, the brand’s virtual workout library, which gives you dozens of programs, like marathon training companions, guided runs, and more. It costs extra after the first 30 days, but I think it’s a distinctive and worthwhile option if you like a guided workout. Of course, you can run on this treadmill without iFit, too.

On to the folding: The frame is huge–it weighs over 300 pounds–so it needs the hydraulic lift help that gets it to fold. The process could be a hair easier, but the balanced weight makes it fairly simple. Moving the 1750, on the other hand, is tricky. Sure, it technically has wheels so that you can roll it around, but that requires tipping the machine and balancing it while you do. Once you place it, you can fold it, but you’re better off leaving it where it is.

The Horizon 7.0AT was the easiest treadmill to get started and learn how to use, but its simplicity holds it back from being the outright best. It’s an old-school treadmill with no touchscreen display or video components, and that limits options for programming. That being said, it’s a very affordable option that gets the job done so long as you don’t need a guided workout or on-board entertainment.

The Horizon 7.0 does exactly what you expect and does a great job of it. It has a 20- by 60-inch running deck that’s plenty large enough for the majority of runners. I wish that it felt a little firmer underfoot, but other members of our team did not have the same complaint. The pre-loaded programs are easy to find if you know your way around a treadmill. (Most of the runners I spoke with are “set and forget” or running with program apps—which you can link through your watch or tablet—so it’s not a worry.) The toggles for speed and incline are intuitive and easy to use.

Folding this one is nice and easy, thanks to a hydraulic assist mechanism. Moving it around is pretty easy, too: The wheels line up in a better place than the 1750. It shrinks by nearly 40 percent when folded, which is genuinely impressive when you consider its massive build and huge incline range. One thing to keep in mind, though: That steep incline lifts you fairly high, so I do not recommend it for basement gyms unless you plan on running flat, or you live in a fancy place with 9-foot basement ceilings.

I’ve never met a treadmill that folds up smaller than the WalkingPad R2. In keeping with the brand, it’s made for walking, with a top speed of 3.7 mph and speed walking at 7.5 mph. And honestly? It’s so compact that you could reasonably put one of these in your home as a more portable complement to a standard, non-folding treadmill without feeling cramped. Use it as an under-desk treadmill or move it around to wherever you can find some free space.

It’s a fantastic treadmill for anyone who wants to get moving when they’d otherwise be sitting around. It features a smaller deck, super-responsive cushioning, and whisper-quiet motor. You could walk on it during a Zoom call with your microphone unmuted, and people would be hard-pressed to hear it. The cushioning means that you’re not going to wear yourself out while you work, and keeps you from bouncing around so badly that you can’t type.

One little thing I like about this folding treadmill is its smart “automatic mode,” which automatically detects your speed changes depending on where your feet are hitting the deck and adjusts as you go. That alone is worth the cost of the machine.

Folding this treadmill is a cinch, and so is storage, thanks to its low weight and small footprint. Even if you store it in a different room from where you use it, it’s only 55 pounds, so you can just haul it from space to space without any issue.

The team at Runner’s World has been testing all things running for decades. We work year-round on everything from shoes to treadmills. Personally, I have been running for over 20 years, running multiple marathons and ultras, and treadmill training is a huge part of my regimen. And I’ve been professionally reviewing products for nearly a decade.

Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate designed a rigorous testing protocol to measure a number of critical features in each and every treadmill that we test, and I wrote a specific rubric to test folding treadmills based on that protocol. This year alone, I have run on over 40 models, racking up almost 200 miles in the past several months. Dengate, who is “never not running,” has also put in miles on many of these models. With folding treadmills, there are several specific qualities we examine to separate the best from the just ok:

Having the ability to fold should not make a treadmill any less useful. While it’s impossible for them to maintain all of the features of certain non-folding treadmills, many or most of them are every bit as good. Some are so gozZod that they even appear on many of our guides.

Even with a compact folding model, it’s important to plan ahead and measure out the spaces where you plan to use and/or store your treadmill. Keep in mind that you need at least 2 feet of clearance surrounding your treadmill in every direction while you’re running. As someone who has put a Cat-shaped hole in the wall of her basement because I lost my footing, I cannot recommend this enough.

There’s a Right Way to Fold and a Wrong Way to Fold

This sounds like a no-brainer, but a folding treadmill should become more compact and easy to store when folded. There are a ton that technically have a folding mechanism but are not all that much smaller in their folded form. If the folded treadmill is too tall for a room, or if it doesn’t clear very much floor space, it doesn’t make sense.

A small running platform can prevent you from feeling comfortable at your full running stride, so we generally think that longer is better. (There are exceptions, of course: A walking pad doesn’t need a long belt.) Width is crucial for people with a wider stride or who tend to wander a bit, or those of us who run a bit duck-footed. A narrow belt can feel constricting when you’re running.

Don’t Worry Too Much About Max Speed and Incline

With folding treadmills especially, you only want as much power as you actually need. A faster max speed requires a bigger motor, which makes for a bigger, heavier treadmill. Most people will be just fine with 10 mph for running, and 3 or 4 mph for walking, so a huge motor isn’t necessary.

Inclines are controlled by a separate motor, so the same rule applies. Most of us don’t want to pretend we’re climbing Everest at the gym, so a 15 percent incline is overkill. It’s nice to have occasionally, but not a dealbreaker to go without.

What are some ways to stay safe on the treadmill while training?

With the treadmill setting the pace for you, it is important to select a pace that you feel capable of walking or running at, and use the safety equipment provided. Be sure you know where the automatic stop switch is and where the speed adjustment buttons are before starting to run/walk.

Should I adjust my mileage while using a treadmill?

Because treadmill running can be easier than road running, you may need to increase your mileage (or adjust speed and incline) when training on the treadmill to get the same level of workout you get from running outdoors. However, many people find treadmill running far less mentally stimulating, making it difficult to do longer distances indoors.

Is a treadmill a good way for newbie runners or walkers to start?

There are benefits of starting your training on a treadmill. The external pacing of the treadmill allows you to set a desired pace, then not have to think about maintaining it once it’s set. Treadmills are also indoors, which means inclement weather can’t stop you from running. They also can have screens attached, allowing you watch shows or follow a video workout instead of just listening to music. However, walking outdoors has been shown to be beneficial for mental health with the changes in scenery as you walk, increased vitamin D production from being in the sun, and decreased sensory stimulation with the absence of screens.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and currently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.
