#8703. Our Editors Rode Dozens of E-Bikes. These 12 Are Worth Buying for Commuting, Trails, Cargo, and Tight Budgets

Find the right e-bike for your ride, budget, and storage needs with our tested top picks.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

You wouldn’t think late autumn is the best time to buy an electric bike; after all, the daylight hours are short, and the weather is getting cold in many regions. However, whether you’re hunting for deals or seeking out the latest tech, now is the time to buy. With holiday discounts and new e-bikes rolling out to dealers and online retailers, plenty of great commuter, cargo, and e-MTB options are out there—at great prices.

I’m a lifelong cyclist, former product director for bike companies, and was a mechanic at busy shops in New York City. Plus, I commute daily on an e-bike and ride test dozens of electric bikes each year. Last summer, I even went almost entirely car-free thanks to an electric cargo bike.

Whether you’re choosing your first e-bike, upgrading to a newer model, or adding another electric model to your garage, dozens of great options are available—and our editors and staff have tested many of them. No matter your age, cycling ability, or budget, brands offer electric bikes that meet needs.

Tip for E-Bike Buyers: Don’t overpay for an electric bike, but spend what you can comfortably afford. If an e-bike is fun to ride, you’ll use it more often. It’s more cost-effective to buy an e-bike equipped the way you want it upfront than to upgrade it later. Also, remember: you cannot change an electric bike’s motor system if you decide you want more power.

The Aventon Level is our benchmark electric bike. It’s a great e-bike for commuting, running errands, or leisure riding. Over several years, the Level platform has proven to be reliable and low-maintenance. Plus, its price doesn’t break the bank.

Aventon split the 4th-generation Level into two models. The REC features a 750W hub motor with 80 Nm of torque. Aventon also added regenerative braking, increasing the bike’s range up to 75 miles. The pricier ADV edition features a mid-drive motor; it bumps up the torque to 100 Nm and range to 110 miles. Both versions come standard with fenders, a rear rack, lights, and suspension.

Another feature users will find quite useful is the Level’s connected features. The Level 4’s ACU (Aventon Control Unit) adds several smart features to the already well-equipped platform. The wheel lock and motion sensor alarm are passive theft deterrents when you stop for a mid-ride coffee or run into the post office. A 4G chip in the ACU enables GPS tracking in Aventon’s mobile app, so you can locate your bike if you forget where you locked it. 4G connectivity also allows you to set geofence restrictions on the bike for teens or housemates.

The relatively affordable seven-speed model Soltera 2.5 from Aventon delivers simplicity and style that is tough to beat. This makes it an excellent choice for getting around town or quick commutes. It’s even better than the original version, thanks to hydraulic disc brakes. A push of the throttle gets you started; then, the brushless hub motor gently assists your pedaling.

Along with disc brakes, the Soltera features integrated lights and turn signals, and the battery is hidden in the bike’s frame (rather than the bolt-on batteries found on many similarly-priced e-bikes). Best for smoother roads and bike paths, the Soltera delivers the essential features a city rider needs in a strikingly light 46-pound package.

Aventon also offers a singlespeed, Soltera 3 ADV with a Gates belt-drive system.

When buying a low-priced e-bike, a simple, low-cost, easy-to-repair, and reliable model usually beats out complicated designs. Lectric’s XP Lite2 is about as basic as it gets. It has a low-maintenance singlespeed drivetrain, a 300-watt hub motor, and a 375Wh battery. With its compact size, 20x2.5-inch tires, and twist-grip throttle, the XP Lite is perfect for zipping through traffic, commuting to the office, or heading to the gym or bar after work.

The XP Lite2 features only one gear and a 300W motor, so it’s not ideal for very hilly terrain. But with the throttle, you can get over small rises and bridges. Lectric also equips the bike with hydraulic disc brakes and front and rear lights. The XP Lite2 is also great for RVers and campgrounds, since it’s lightweight (about 48 pounds) and folds down to 36x16x27-inch dimensions.

Many “step-through” e-bikes don’t actually have a low step design. This makes it challenging for some riders to mount or dismount. However, the CTY e2.1, by REI’s Co-op house brand, has a fully step-through front triangle. The CTY is a great choice for older riders, those with reduced mobility, or others who seek an easy-to-ride e-bike.

REI equips the CTY e2.1 with a 250-watt hub-drive motor that provides smooth pedal-assistance up to 20 mph. It also features a suspension fork to smooth out bumps and potholes, an adjustable stem for a comfortable riding position, and hydraulic disc brakes for better stopping. For less than the cost of some e-bikes online, you can get a quality electric bike backed up by REI warranty and service.

The Current ADV is the priciest bike in this story, but for a good reason. Some electric bikes look a lot like mountain bikes, but that doesn’t mean they are built for real off-road use. Aventon’s new Current is the brand’s first full suspension E-MTB, and it is trail-ready right out of the box. Trevor Raab, Bicycling’s Senior Photographer and Test Team member, said, “The bike’s intuitive ride feel will please experienced mountain bikers and also benefit first-time mountain bikers.”

The Current ADV features an aluminum frame with 140mm rear wheel travel and a great-feeling motor with 750 peak Watts and 110 Nm of torque. (It also has a Boost mode that bumps power to 850W and 120 Nm of torque.) Rounding out the ADV are high-end components like a RockShox Psylo Gold fork, SRAM DB8 brakes, SRAM Eagle 70 Mechanical transmission, and a tubeless wheelset with Maxxis Minion EXO tires.

In his full review of the bike, “Aventon Goes Full Performance: The Current Electric Mountain Bike Is Surprisingly Dialed,” Raab particularly likes the Current’s easy-to-use interface. It’s loaded with ride data as well as the ability to tune the motor settings. If you don’t need rear suspension, check out Aventon’s updated Ramblas ADV hardtail E-MTB.

READ AVENTON CURRENT REVIEWMORE GREAT E-MTBs

Getting into E-MTB trail riding on a budget is tough. Low-priced electric mountain bikes often aren’t built strong enough for off-road riding (or weigh half a rider’s weight), and trail-capable models typically cost more than $4,000. That’s what makes the TrailRush a standout bike—for less than $2,000, you get a trail-ready hardtail you can take on singletrack and have some fun.

Ride1Up equips the 29-inch-wheeled TrailRush with a Brose mid-drive motor. With 90 Nm of torque, it isn’t as powerful as many new, higher-priced E-MTB motors, but it gets the job done. The TrailRush also comes stock with a dropper seatpost, four-piston disc brakes, and tubeless-compatible rims with Maxxis Minion tires.

Of course, to hit this great price, Ride1Up made some equipment sacrifices. The 504Wh battery isn’t as large as some peers (like the Aventon Ramblas), so you get less ride time between charges. Additionally, the 11-36T cassette and 38T chainring limit your ability to climb steep hills.

Compared to earlier iterations of the Aventure, the third-generation model has a smoother ride and feels more like a premium bike (without the high price tag). Aventon’s new torque sensor allows more control over the acceleration of Aventure’s 750W rear hub motor. Lighter-weight testers found earlier models had too much torque, but this Aventure remedied that fault. Additional features include a new head-unit interface, integrated turn signals, a front light, a rear rack, and fenders.

The Aventure 3 is an excellent fat-tire e-bike for commuters—especially on snowy days and gravel paths. Off-roading, it excels on doubletrack trails and cinder paths, but with this burly bike’s weight and components, it has limited functionality on singletrack and more aggressive mountain trails.

Aventon also offers the Aventure M, a mid-drive version of the Aventure. It keeps the same big, burly character but adds a more premium feel, a smoother, more powerful motor, and an upgraded drivetrain—along with a higher price. Those refinements cost about $1,000 more than the Aventure 3.

Buying an e-bike on Amazon can be risky, especially if you don’t know much about bikes or have limited mechanical experience. However, sometimes you can find a good deal on a decent bike. At $500, the Heybike Cityscape isn’t the pinnacle of e-bike technology, but it lets you get out and enjoy some rides without breaking the bank.

I combed through dozens of Amazon listings comparing low-priced electric bikes, and this Heybike stood out for its combination of price and features. Then, I saw someone on the local bike path with one and asked them about the bike. The rider liked it and said it has been trouble-free (they noted a local bike shop assembled it for them). Heybike’s U.S. support line is available for warranty service or product questions.

Don’t want to purchase from Amazon? Use this exclusive Bicycling discount link for $100 (applied at checkout) off the Cityscape 2.0, plus free shipping.

Tern’s cargo bikes are the gold standard for practical features, durability, and ride quality. This reputation makes the brand’s GSD (longtail) and HSD (short-tail) cargo models top picks for bike commuters, families, and riders looking to cut their dependence on automobiles.

The new third-generation HSD improves on its predecessor’s legacy. The HSD (short for “Haul Stuff Daily”) is a shrunken-down version of Tern’s GSD3 model released last year. The HSD3’s frame has a 419-pound carrying capacity (combined bike, rider, and cargo), added stiffness, and improved stability at speed compared to its predecessor. The P10e Sport configuration features the peppier Bosch Performance Line Sport motor and an electronic-shifting ten-speed TRP E.A.S.I. A10 drivetrain. The Sport motor’s 28mph assistance was a welcome upgrade for commuting and running errands alongside car traffic on local suburban streets. The 90 Nm of torque (15 Nm more than the standard Performance Line motor) also provides quicker acceleration from a dead stop and a little more oomph when loaded down with cargo or climbing hills.

While it’s the second-most affordable HSD3 model in Tern’s U.S. selection, the P10e Sport is certainly not a budget-priced e-bike. But for the extra cost over similar-sized cargo bikes, you get a proven and well-thought-out bicycle. The HSD’s features and design elements feel purposeful. A great example of this is the bike’s stowability: The HSD3 can be tilted and stored vertically, balanced on its rear rack. It also moves easily on its rear wheel when you need to park or store it. The handlebar and stem also fold down, making the HSD3 much easier to transport by car or SUV than almost any other e-bike.

Many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Currently priced at $1,399 for the single-battery model, it boasts an impressive 60-mile range and a top speed of 28 mph. (The dual-battery model for $1,799 doubles the range to 120 miles.) This makes the XPedition one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes around and a good option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike.

“The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, said Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers ($150) and the Essentials package ($120), I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”

However, to reach a price like this, concessions have to be made somewhere. This results in a somewhat cheap feeling to the bike. Most of the XPedition’s parts are bottom-tier—with the notable exception of the brakes. The pedal-assist motor is powerful off the line, but at times, it feels erratic. The XPedition is adequate if you live in a very flat area or don’t need to carry kids or an adult passenger. Despite these faults, if you’re on a budget and looking to ditch the car for errands and trips around town, the XPedition is the cheapest e-cargo bike we recommend buying.

Plenty of commuter e-bikes cost far less than Specialized’s Turbo Vado SL 2, and they can probably do most of these things. So why spend twice as much as many popular options? I dive into the details in my story, “Stop Wasting Money on Cheap E-Bikes. Here’s Why Spending More Pays Off for Commuters.”

The TL;DR: The Turbo Vado SL 2’s excellent ride geometry, silky-smooth motor, low weight, and premium components make riding fun. Together, these features make you want to ride the Vado every day and use it for more than simply getting to work. And thanks to Specialized’s extensive dealer network, you have somewhere to turn when it needs service.

“Lightweight e-bike” might sound like an oxymoron to some, but a sub-40-pound weight is impressive when many electric bikes exceed 60 or 80 pounds. And often, e-bikes this light are pricey. Yet, the Velotric Tempo is only $1,499 and boasts a 39 lb. (claimed) weight.

Velotric achieves this weight reduction by ditching the bulky suspension fork (suspension forks on lower-priced bikes often don’t work all that well, to be frank), swapping heavy tires for 700x42c gravel tires, and using a smaller battery. Riders who need to carry the bike up any stairs or load it onto a bike rack will appreciate the reduced weight. However, heavier riders may want to test ride the Tempo before purchase, as lower-powered motors can bog down and reduce battery range for bigger-bodied people.

Bicycles are my life, and I’m a dedicated e-bike user and enthusiast. I’ve also worked in cycling for over 25 years. For almost six years, I’ve ridden and tested electric bikes as Bicycling’s Deputy Editor—and I use e-bikes for my daily commute. Before joining the staff, I led product development for top bicycle brands.

Our editors test dozens of electric bikes across every cycling category, and we continually receive new models to evaluate. Our riding involves much more than taking bikes on short spins; we use electric bikes in our daily lives. Commuting, school drop-offs, grocery runs, and daily transportation are only a few of the things we regularly do with e-bikes. We also hit the trails on E-MTB models to test their performance in real-world mountain biking conditions, not simply riding them around town.

In addition to ride-testing, our editors regularly talk to cyclists of all ages and abilities about their riding needs. This helps us craft our list of Best Electric Bikes: e-bikes that will meet your needs on the street, trails, and around the neighborhood. Two of the e-bikes in this story even made the final cut for our 2026 Bike Awards.

Electric bike prices range from entry-level models for less than $500 to premium machines costing almost as much as a good used car. However, our years of testing have proven that many of the best and most practical models live squarely in the middle.

We find that many standout e-bikes are priced between $1,500 and $3,000. These models strike a good balance between reliability and practicality, without requiring you to overspend on features or technology you don’t need. Electric bikes costing less than $1,000 often take shortcuts to achieve this, either by using lower-quality parts or offering limited service after the bike is purchased.

Of course, you can also spend much more on electric bikes. Premium e-bikes typically offer improved motor performance, higher-quality components, lower weight, or more tech features. However, for most general riding purposes, these bikes are overkill—but they‘re certainly fun!

→ Consider how much cargo you’ll need to carry if your riding involves commuting or running errands. Look for a bike with appropriate racks, mount points, and other accessories.

→ For singletrack and trail riding, look for mountain bikes with knobby tires, adjustable suspension, high-quality frames, and low weight.

→ Pay attention to weight. While fat tire e-bikes and cargo bikes offer versatility, many weigh over 90 pounds. If you’ll need to carry your bike up any stairs or lift it onto a bike rack, a lighter option will be a better fit.

→ Bike storage is another consideration. While most e-bikes don’t require excessive space compared to their non-pedal-assisted counterparts, ensure you have access to a power outlet where you plan to store it for easy charging.

Several e-bike brands, Aventon, Ride1Up, and Lectric, performed well in our ride testing and evaluations. These bikes might require some minor assembly at home, such as installing pedals, a seat, and tightening handlebars. We considered how easy bikes were to assemble in our recommendations. Many bike shops will not assemble or otherwise work on e-bikes they do not sell due to liability issues. The direct-to-consumer brands we recommend have dealers nationwide ready to support you.

Established bike companies, such as Specialized and Trek, manufacture e-bikes and have hundreds of dealers across North America. Additionally, REI sells its house-brand Co-op electric bikes (and models from Cannondale and Tern) in its stores.

There are three electric-assist classes available in the United States, and the use of each class of bike can vary by state, city, and area you are riding. Be sure to check local regulations before buying and before riding your bike.

Class 1: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Class 2: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle comes standard equipment.

Class 3: 28 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment

What this means: Class 1 motors kick in only when you pedal and stop helping you at 20 mph. Class 2 also offers pedal assist up to 20 mph, but these bikes can also have a throttle-powered mode that allows users to engage the motor without pedaling. Class 3 is pedal-assist like Class 1, but helps you until you reach 28 mph.

Other countries classify electric bikes differently, and many do not allow e-bikes to assist riders beyond 20 miles per hour.

Electric bikes generally feature one of two types of motors: mid-drive motors, which are contained in the frame at the bottom of the bike between the pedals; and rear hub motors, which are built into the rear wheel.

Bikes with rear hub motors are generally less expensive but are also less powerful. Mid-drive e-bikes tend to be more expensive, but are typically more reliable and higher performance. Because the extra weight on a mid-drive motor is centered in the bike and lower to the ground, these bikes are generally easier to handle than bikes with hub motors.

Measured in Newton meters (or Nm), torque is a rotational measurement of force—and the number to pay attention to when you want an idea of an e-bike motor’s output. More torque means more power off the line and more boost to your pedaling.

The heavier the bike, the more torque it needs. Lighter road bikes typically have 30 to 40 Nm of torque, and trail and cargo models (generally) have at least 80 Nm. Most commuter bikes fall somewhere in between.

The size of an e-bike’s battery is measured in watt-hours (or Wh). This measurement represents the energy stored in the battery and how many watts it can deliver each hour. The higher the number, the longer the range, but the faster you go, the faster you drain the battery.

So, if a 504Wh battery paired with a 500W motor gives you one hour of ride time at the highest assist, riding at about half that power will double your range.

Many e-bike brands seamlessly integrate batteries to make the bike look sleeker (and more like a traditional non-assist bike). Most batteries lock to the bike and come with a key that lets you unlock and remove it, which serves multiple purposes: You can remove the battery and charge it off the bike, plus a locked battery deters (and hopefully prevents) a thief from stealing it. An e-bike with the battery removed is safer for hauling on a bike rack and lighter for carrying up steps.

Since e-bikes can maintain higher speeds for longer than standard bikes, you want extra control when riding. Wider tires provide better traction and the freedom to leave the pavement with little penalty, and a suspension fork will help tame some of the rougher roads you might explore. Good disc brakes are a must, too, for slowing a heavy bike at high speed. This is not a place to skimp.

Some e-bikes have an integrated lighting system that turns on when you power up the bike. While this is a great feature, it’s not a deal-breaker if your bike doesn’t come equipped this way. It’s just as easy to attach your own since so many great bike lights are available.

E-bikes need regular maintenance and repair to stay in good working condition. Because they’re heavier and go faster than non-assist bicycles, e-bikes often require more regular service on parts like brakes, tires, and drivetrain components. We recommend having a good relationship with a local bike shop experienced in e-bike repair to keep your equipment running smoothly.

E-bikes use electronics for their motors, batteries, and displays. These parts are often proprietary to bike brands or even specific e-bike models, making replacement more difficult than parts on non-electric bicycles. Make sure to use the correct electronic replacement parts to avoid damaging your e-bike (or it catching fire).

Established brands usually (but not always) have a good supply of these parts for replacement, even for years after a bike goes out of production. Bosch and Shimano are two e-bike motor manufacturers with some of the most compatibility between bikes and stock parts for previous generations of systems.

Look for e-bikes from brands that offer at least a one-year warranty on electronic components (many brands’ warranties are longer) and make items like replacement batteries for your bike. These parts are usually not cheap (sometimes up to half the cost of a new bike), but it’s the difference between having an e-bike that can be repaired or becomes a bicycle-shaped paperweight if something goes wrong.

Following a dramatic increase in fires caused by the lithium-ion batteries used in electric bikes, there is a push from local officials, regulatory agencies, and advocacy groups across the U.S. for improved safety certification of e-bikes, batteries, and motor units. In September 2023, a New York City law took effect requiring that any e-bike sold in the city “has been certified by an accredited testing laboratory for compliance with Underwriters Laboratories (UL) standard 2849”.

However, just because something is marketed as UL 2849 compliant, tested to UL 2849, or even “certified to UL 2849” does not mean it is UL Safety Certified. Ibrahim Jilani, UL’s Global Director of Consumer Technology, notes: “Certification is always earned by a manufacturer and not a given when they undergo a product submittal. The UL Mark, or any authorized certification mark, can only be issued upon successful demonstration of meeting the requirements of the safety standard.” You can find UL’s updated list of products certified to UL 2849 here. You can cross-reference OSHA’s Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratories for a deep dive into the topic.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8702. The 8 Best Running Gloves for Logging Cold-Weather Miles

Not feeling the tips of your fingers on a run is unacceptable—these gloves provide wind resistance and warmth.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 23, 2026: Several gloves on this list are on sale, including our Best Value, the Nike Pacer. Some pairs are low in stock, including the Ibex Kilometer Glove, which is only available in small. We will update accordingly as brands roll out their new winter inventory.

The first snowfall can be magical, but overcast skies and visible breath during a run can dampen the enthusiasm of any runner impatient for spring. To survive the everlasting cold, the trick is to layer properly so you don’t feel miserable during winter training. Stocking up on a winter running jacket, leggings, and pants is a no-brainer, but don’t forget to accessorize. I’m talking gloves here.

As a constantly cold person who has three sweatshirts piled onto the back of her office desk chair, I’ll never forget that one Santa 5-Miler when I left my gloves in my car. As I squeezed my hands into fists trying to retain warmth as I raced, I swore to never again run a winter race without full coverage over my five digits.

This winter has tested my cold-weather tolerance, dipping below zero degrees Fahrenheit more than once. But it’s a perfect breeding ground for glove—and mitten—testing. Here are my top picks.

I’ve worked at RW for eight years and started running XC in high school. I learned to embrace the cold this year, testing most of the gloves included on this list. I judged them by insulation, dexterity, and fit. I also had a little help from male staffers, who tested the men’s version of gloves—and became aghast learning that the women’s wasn’t similar.

Contributor Nick Hilden also provides tips on what to look for when shopping for gloves and answers your frequently asked questions on when to wear them, and on sizing and fit.

The Smartwool Active Fleece Insulated Glove is included in our Best Winter Gear for Runners guide because it checks off all the boxes: double-knit insulation, reflective lining, windproof panels, and touchscreen-compatible fingertips. The stitching on the long cuffs ensures a secure, tailored fit around the wrists.

The Active Fleece kept my fingers warm for an hour during 32-degree and slightly below freezing runs. When the temperature dropped to 20, my fingers started to ache after a half hour in the cold.

My main critique is that they’re unisex sizing only. Even the smallest size, extra small, left some room above my fingertips, which made it difficult to grasp items I pocketed and zippers. The patch on the palm didn’t reach past my thumb and forefinger, which would have provided a soft area for nose wiping.

Smartwool Active Fleece Insulated Glove Review

These gloves by the Swoosh are great for easing into cold weather. The sizing is sex-specific and true-to-size. They’re favorable for their sleek construction, making dexterity possible when you need to refuel midrun—or just grab your apartment key—and don’t want to remove your gloves.

Because of their thinness, your fingertips may start to ache once the thermometer hits below freezing. Still, they’re a great pair when you’re transitioning into colder weather or have a higher threshold to the cold.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

When you’re pitting gloves against mittens, it’s dexterity versus warmth. Gloves allow you to use your fingers, but mittens keep them together, thereby minimizing heat loss.

Even though I felt like I was running with oven mitts on my hands (the sizing is small/medium, medium/large), the Convertible Zip Mittens were great for braving workouts that dipped into the teens—and tens. The extra room also allows for doubling up if you really want to head out when it’s minus 1 degree Fahrenheit or less.

The Velcro tabs allow you to tighten the fit around the wrists, and the interior lining feels as plush as the felt on my very authentic Robin Hood hat from Nottingham.

If you’re prone to losing a mate when things come in pairs, TrailHeads sees you: a buckle guarantees your left and right mitt won’t be separated. Afraid of losing both mitts? Attach them to a carabiner on your duffel using the loops on the cuffs. The reflective zipper is a nice touch if you need to use your fingers midrun.

My one issue with the mittens: the material on the thumbs leaves snot trails.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com

My coworkers thought I was heading out on the slopes or wearing garden gloves, but the Ibex Kilometer isn’t just for skiers (or gardeners). After a stretch of testing during a brief stay in New York City, the Kilometer gets my runner seal of approval. I tested them while logging runs in Central Park and the Hudson River Greenway, hitting gusts of wind on rolling hills and by the water. Temperatures varied from 20 to 40 degrees Fahrenheit; the Kilometer made my workouts more bearable.

The leather palms had excellent grip when I ran holding my phone, trying to find the best route back to my hotel. My fingers were shielded from the river’s wind chill and the ribbed cuffs kept my wrists toasty. But the biggest win for me was the soft, absorbent patch of fabric on each thumb. They were perfect for swiping my very runny nose when the wind speed was 15 mph.

If you run with your phone and whip it out a bunch of times midrun, these are your gloves; almost the entire palm is patterned with silicone grips. The fingertips are touchscreen-compatible and sizing is sex-specific, which translates to no bunched fingers or agitation trying to scroll.

These gloves aren’t for extreme weather, but they’re great when things start to get nippy or when you’re heading out for a short winter run. However, there’s one thing TrailHeads must rectify: It’s a travesty that only the men’s version has a nose wipe patch. Why did they skimp on this feature with the women’s edition?

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com

These aren’t the cotton gloves you wore in grade school. The Smartwool Liner offers so much more in terms of warmth and quality; it all starts with the woven material.

The fabric is merino wool, which regulates warmth, controls odors, and dries fast. The fingertips are touchscreen-compatible, and you’re not limited to a small patch on the thumb when you need to wipe your nose (the glove itself is real estate). The ribbed cuffs fit snug, even on small wrists. They’re great to wear when the temperature is mid-30s; maybe even lower if you don’t have near-Raynaud’s hands like mine.

Despite coming in unisex with no extra-small option, I was surprised how well the small Vortex Gloves fit my hands and how easy it was to use my phone and text. The fleece layer feels soft on my skin and I’ll honestly never understand why a glove/mitt hybrid is so underrated. The mitten hood serves as wind protection; it’s great on gusty runs or when the temperature slowly rises. You can tuck in the entire hood above the wrist, with the hi-vis tape still partially showing.

The gloves aren’t for extreme cold, however. I ran in the Vortex Windblock when the temperature dipped in the teens and not even the mitt hood could stop my fingers from aching. That’s not the worst knock, since we’ve had abnormal weather below 10 degrees and most gloves on this list either didn’t make the cut or only lasted for half an hour before I had to ball my hands in the palms.

The Vortex Windblock also has snaps on the cuffs so you can store them attached.

Prone to losing your gloves? The snap on the lululemon Fast and Free prevents accidental separation and it’s just one standout reason you should buy this pair.

These sleek gloves have silicone grippers to keep you from dropping your phone midrun midtext, as well as “screen-conductive” finger pads that allow you to use your touchscreen.

Striking reflectivity details the back of the Fast and Free. That fabric is also soft enough to swipe your nose without causing the skin on your nostrils to peel.

Shop Men’s at shop.lululemon.com | Shop Women’s at lululemon.com

Winter runners should look for a pair of lightweight gloves that are warm enough to keep your hands cozy, but breathable enough to let air circulate. Look for technical fabrics—polyester and other synthetic materials are often your best bet for finding that balance.

Some blends are better than others though. In case of bad weather, it also makes sense to keep an eye out for a weather-resistant material that can protect against rain and snow, as well as cold, cutting winds. Moisture-wicking materials, such as merino wool, can also help deal with sweat and mitigate the impact of cold rain.

I also like when a glove fabric contains a small amount of a stretchy material, such as spandex or elastane, to ensure the gloves fit comfortably and snug. That said, skip the stretch if you like a glove that feels roomy inside.

On the other hand, I recommend avoiding heavy gloves made from nylon or polyurethane. These materials are often thicker, warmer and weatherproof, so they’re more likely to make you overheat. (Depending on the design, they may also make it hard to use your phone or check your smartwatch.)

Everyone has their own Goldilocks spot for how much warmth they need from their gloves. The important thing to keep in mind is that your body feels warmer while you’re running–speaking broadly, we recommend dressing for a run as if it's 10- to 20 degrees warmer than the temperature outside (including the wind chill.) That’s a good rubric for determining both when to start wearing gloves in the winter, and the level of protection you want against the cold.

Thinking about gloves specifically, your running gloves probably shouldn’t be as warm as your everyday winter gloves. A warmer glove will keep you going in colder temperatures but will cause you to sweat more, so it may not feel comfortable for long.

Winter nights come early, so visibility is an essential concern for all cold-weather running gear. If you frequently run near a road, or in areas with little street lighting, every item of clothing you wear, head to toe, should feature a reflective or high-visibility element.

In fact, gloves are among the most important pieces of reflective running gear you can wear. They catch drivers’ eyes especially well because your hands move as you run, creating a more noticeable effect.

When should I start wearing running gloves in the winter?

Every person feels differently about gloves, but as I said earlier in the piece, experts recommend dressing for a run as if it’s 10 degrees warmer than the effective temperature with the wind chill. If you normally wear gloves on a 50-degree day, start putting on gloves when it’s 40 degrees.

A good running glove should fit snug around your hand. If there’s room for your hand to move inside the glove, your skin may rub against the fabric and start to chafe. At the same time, it’s important to make sure they aren’t too tight, which might reduce circulation.

One way to check if you have the right fit is by doing a pinch test. Put on one glove, then pinch the fabric at the tip of a finger with your other hand. Ideally, you should have about a quarter inch of extra room.

Most glove brands use one of two measurements to determine sizing: The circumference of your fingers at the knuckles (without the thumb), and full hand length from the base of the hand to the tip of the middle finger. Check the product listing on the glove to see how the brand measures.

To measure the knuckle circumference, hold your fingers together, then wrap a measuring tape around your knuckles. Don’t squeeze your fingers too tight, though.

When measuring your full hand, make sure your middle finger is fully extended to ensure a proper measurement.

#8701. The Real Grand Theft

Editor-in-chief Chris Foster on why Grand Theft Auto 6 costs more than you think (Photo: Donald Miralle/Getty Images)

Everything has a price, and I think the cost of Grand Theft Auto 6 — the much-anticipated sixth installment of one of the most successful video games in history — is far too high.

And I’m not talking about the cost to your wallet.

Triathletes know all about expensive things: Tri bikes now start around $3,000 and rise (quickly) up from there; running shoes now routinely crack $200; and now we’ve got $270 swim caps. And don’t even get me started on entry fees — the 2026 Hawaii Ironman World Championship, for instance, topped $1,800, granted that’s easily our sport’s crown jewel, but even a new event like 70.3 Utah still rings in around $500.

And even once you factor in the hard out-of-pocket expenses for equipment, entry fees, pool access, coaching, travel, accommodations, and so on, there’s still that looming cost of your time.

If a midpack triathlete did our most popular 70.3 training plan, they’d spend about 150 hours of training over the 20-week plan. For our 16-week Olympic-distance plan, a triathlete would rack up about 65 hours of training. That’s a pretty big chunk of life, but I know I’m preaching to the choir, as all triathletes know that our sport requires a big time commitment.

However, there’s good news: We know that much of that time can be spent outside; we know that — when done correctly — swimming, biking, and running are very healthy endeavors; and we know that much of that time can be spent with others. To that last point, for better or for worse, even just the act of going to a race forces us to participate within a community.

In a digital world that competes ferociously for our attention (think: social media, TV, AI, and so on), giving your precious and valuable attention — your time — to swimming, biking, running, and triathlon will do more for your physical and mental health than getting hooked and strung out on a screen for hours.

So it’s here, in the obsession over the release of GTA 6, that as the leader of an outdoor-related title — and within the context of an era of critically dangerous social disconnection and physical isolation — I find myself confused about why the larger culture is celebrating the creation of something that will drain our attention and time like a dystopian plug in the back of a Matrix battery-person’s skull. I just can’t celebrate.

On one hand, a video game centered on crime and violence is probably more of a sign of the times than a cause for rising crime rates in real life. I’ll succumb to a little bit of Qoheleth-level despair recognizing here that “what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun.”

And of course this is an outdoor sports publication, not Morality Weekly, but I still can’t shake another quote from the bestselling book of all time: “The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness.”

GTA 6’s content notwithstanding, from my position in outdoor/endurance sports, I certainly can’t quite abide when our culture treats the release of a video game like a high holy holiday. Especially when it comes at such a high cost.

Set aside the hard price tag of a gaming console and game (let’s say less than $1k), which is actually relatively low compared to a hobby like triathlon, and keep your eyes fixed on the time cost and quality.

Experts from IGN note that Grand Theft Auto 6 took their editors between 42 and 115 hours to complete the new release. It’s probably a good guess that the average gamer would spend 80ish hours to noodle around in that virtual environment. That’s a lot of “life spend.”

And unlike many other video games, it’s time spent, well…alone.

GTA 6 has no multiplayer mode as of this writing (though it could come). This means there’s no opportunity to connect with other people — even remotely — during gameplay. You can’t commit crimes alongside your buddies in the living room; you can’t fire at police alongside friends in Sweden, Hong Kong, or France. You’re alone, for 60 hours, stealing cars and shooting people. You interact only with that world and the characters coded into it.

Now I won’t be entirely obtuse here — not everyone can physically train for a triathlon; not everyone has time or safe access to a place where they can spend 65-150 hours outdoors, even if they wanted to.

However, there is a large proportion of people whose time spent playing a video game (alone) will prevent them from being outside (with others) — moving their bodies through nature in some way, shape, or form.

That’s why, rather than relish the empty streets and bike paths that have been reported across major metropolitan areas this week, I’ll be hoping that once the game ends and the credits roll (do video games have credits?), folks will head back outside to get a refund for time better spent.

#8700. The One Piece of Cold-Weather Gear I Never Leave at Home

It’s cheap, packable, and useful enough that I bring it even when the forecast looks mild.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

From 55 degrees down to 25, I bring one piece of cold-weather gear on every ride: a neck buff. It isn’t the most exciting item in my kit, and it won’t make a dramatic difference in a gear photo. But it’s useful across a wider range of temperatures than almost anything else I own, and it costs far less than most winter gear cyclists spend serious money on.

At 55 degrees, I can wear it loosely around my neck and cut the wind without feeling bundled up. As the temperature drops, that little bit of insulation becomes more valuable. Covering your neck makes you feel warmer, and the buff also helps close the gap at the top of your jacket. Cold air sneaking in around the collar can make an otherwise reasonable layering setup feel inadequate. A buff helps keep that draft out.

When it gets really cold, I pull it up over my ears and face. It’s a simple way to add coverage without committing to a heavier balaclava for the whole ride. And if the temperature changes, or I start working harder on a climb, I can pull it back down in a few seconds. It takes up almost no space in a jersey pocket, which means there’s little reason to leave it at home.

Neck buffs grew out of a practical problem familiar to motorcycle riders: keeping cold, wind, and road dust off your neck and face. Riders already used bandanas and other neck cloths; the stretchy tube made that protection easier to wear under a helmet. Skiers adopted it too, which may be why people associate it with snow sports.

There is no shortage of expensive cycling accessories that promise to keep you warm while riding. Many are quite good. But few come close to the humble neck buff in terms of how practical, simple, and cheap it is. It’s an adaptable piece of kit that’s just as useful on a cool ride that doesn’t quite call for full winter kit as it is on a truly cold ride, when every gap and exposed bit of skin becomes a problem. It’s a small thing, which is exactly why I never leave home without it.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. #8699. 5 Yoga Poses to Get You Through Any Holiday Gathering

Certain seasons come with a lot, and we mean a lot, of socializing. On the one hand, this means a chance to spend quality time with family and friends, which is always a win. But if you deal with any amount of social anxiety, gatherings can also come with stress and general overwhelm.

If leaving isn’t an option—just kidding, we know you probably want to be there—there are ways to find grounding and calm within your own being. You can practice breathwork, take a walk, even excuse yourself and enjoy a yoga pose or two for a minute. Or, if you resonate with the asanas on this list, perhaps five!

These yoga poses are meant to be easily accessible. Escape for a few moments to try one of the more involved poses or enjoy a super subtle modification mid-party!

Holiday gatherings tend to involve a fair amount of standing around—which is where your casual Tree Pose (Vrksasana) comes in. Popping one foot up—whether against your upper or lower leg or, more stealthily, your ankle—can be done at literally any time: while you’re doing the dishes, chatting with loved ones, or experiencing a lull in activity. The reminder that you’re in control of your sense of balance can help you feel steadier on your own two feet in all ways.

Folding forward can provide a sense of tremendous release and relief. Hinging at your hips in Standing Forward Bend (Uttanasana) and allowing your head and upper body to hang heavy—sometimes referred to as Rag Doll—serves as a subtle inversion, activating your parasympathetic nervous system and encouraging calm. Plus, this pose is normal enough to fold into at any point. Just tell your people that you need a quick stretch.

Finding strength within yourself can make chilling out a little easier. Pressing up—or jumping back—into Plank Pose activates your core, arms, and legs, then asks you to pause. Turning your focus toward this physical task, whether for a few breaths or a full minute, can help snap you out of an anxious spin and get you back into a celebratory state.

Sometimes, the best thing you can do is retreat to a spare bedroom (or the couch or the floor) and lie down for a while. Savasana can certainly provide some calming release, but for something a little more likely to get you out of your head and into your body, try Reclining Bound Angle Pose. It’s a subtle stretch that rejuvenates without being daunting—sort of like a best-case-scenario social engagement.

#8698. Zwift Ride Drops to $999 for Black Friday—A Complete Indoor Bike Our Editors Picked Over Pricier Trainers

A complete Zwift-ready bike and our favorite Wahoo trainer are both on sale now at deep discounts.

As cyclists, the end of November usually means two things: A shift to riding the indoor trainer and scoring Black Friday deals on cycling gear. This year, Zwift combines them for big savings on the Zwift Ride and the Wahoo Kickr Core 2. These are Bicycling’s two best-tested trainers, available for up to 23% off!

The Ride is an indoor training bike designed for seamless integration with Zwift’s popular virtual cycling platform—it’s a bicycle and trainer in one, you don’t even need to attach your outdoor bike. If you want to use your own bicycle to ride in Watopia or train inside this winter, Zwift also has an great deal on our top-rated smart trainer, the Wahoo Kickr Core 2.

Training bikes are quickly gaining popularity among indoor riders. These purpose-built units integrate a bike and trainer for quick set up, easy use, and improved durability. With a training bike, you no longer have to fumble to get your bike on the trainer on a rainy day, swap bikes when a family member wants to ride Zwift, or prematurely wear out components on your pricey road, gravel, or mountain bike.

Until Zwift introduced its Ride bike, price has been the big downside to training bikes. Popular models are $2,500 to $4,000; the Ride $1,300 everyday price cut that cost in half—Zwift’s Black Friday deal trims drops the price to only $999. That’s a complete, Zwift-ready indoor bike for less than the price of some direct drive trainers.

How does Zwift do it? Instead of over-thinking things, Zwift combines the excellent Wahoo Kickr Core 2 smart trainer with a stripped down bicycle frame. But instead of building up this frame with pricey components that wear out quickly, it uses a robust singlespeed drivetrain and shift levers with built-in controls for use on the Zwift platform.

The Ride also features easily adjustable seat height, handlebar height, and bar reach. If you want to use your own saddle or a different bar, the Ride uses standard sizing for easy swaps. Zwift also recently updated Ride with crank length options and more fore-aft saddle adjustment. This means almost anyone can fit on the bike, and it makes it easy to share the Ride with multiple riders in your home.

Seeing the price, it’s easy to assume the Zwift Ride’s low price means a lower-quality experience. However, in head-to-head testing against much more expensive training bikes, the Ride walked away as our editors’ clear pick for most indoor cyclists.

Wahoo’s best-priced indoor trainer is actually the brand’s best overall. The Kickr Core 2 packs all of the accuracy, simplicity, and power of the range-topping Kickr smart trainer into a better-priced package. As Test Editor Dan Chabanov stated in his full length review, “The Core 2 delivers nearly all of the real-world experience of Wahoo’s flagship trainer at a price that’s roughly 50 percent lower.” And that’s saying a lot: Chabanov is a former elite cyclocross and road racer, and still competes at a high-level in Zwift’s racing leagues.

The Kickr Core 2 is a great deal at its everyday price of $550, and at $400 it’s a steal! The Core 2 features a smooth 11.9-pound flywheel with up to 1,800 watts max resistance, 16-percent gradient simulation, and quick connections via BlueTooth and ANT+ protocols. For updates and smooth data connection, Wahoo added WiFi connectivity to the Core trainer. It also features Zwift Race Mode for better connection and data transfer when racing online.

The 30 pound Kickr Core 2 fits bikes with 130mm and 135mm quick release dropouts or thru axle-equipped bikes with 142mm or 148mm dropout spacing. The Core 2 has more stable legs than the original model; they work well for all but elite-level sprint efforts. Compared to the top-tier Kickr, the Core 2’s only downsides are its lack of a carrying handle and that it doesn’t fold as small for storage.

This version of the Kickr Core 2 also includes Zwift’s Cog and Click system. The singlespeed Cog replaces a traditional cassette and works with 8- to 13-speed drivetrains. This means you can use most bikes onto the Core 2 without worrying about cassette compatibility—it‘s great for riders who train indoors on multiples bikes (for example, a gravel bike one day and a road bike another ride) or for households with more than one user.

The Click is two small video game-style controllers you mount to your bar to virtually shift your bike in Zwift. The buttons also can award kudos, use power-ups, and scroll menus inside Zwift’s Watopia universe.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). #8697. After a Decade of Refusing to Use a Treadmill, I Finally Gave In. Here’s How It’s Making Me a Better Runner.

Cold, dark days don’t have to derail your running. The treadmill might be the fix you need.

When the weather dipped below freezing for the first time last winter and the sun began to set at 4:30 p.m., I knew I’d have to leave my typical after-work miles behind. Cold weather and early darkness have always been an easy one-two punch to my running motivation.

I’d also long held another line in the sand: I didn’t run on treadmills—at least not since high school gym class. I took to calling myself a “purist” because I didn’t think running was worth it if it wasn’t outside in nature. I believed my cause was noble, but really, I was just piling up excuses not to run in the winter.

So I decided to give treadmill running a chance. I set out to complete one to two easy runs per week for a month to see if it could help me stay consistent through the winter. Within a few weeks, I was running more than I ever had in winters past—and reconsidering what held me back all those years.

My experiment started after work in late fall. I turned to one of the Bowflex treadmills we have at Runner’s World headquarters. Earlier in the day, my editor casually mentioned that my Apple Watch would sync directly to the treadmill for a more accurate reading, a suggestion that made me more excited to get started on my test.

I walked up to the treadmill and the first thing I noticed was that if I wanted to, I could put my Netflix password into the built-in monitor and fire up an episode of Brooklyn Nine-Nine for the 200th time. While this capability isn’t very advanced as far as treadmill features go nowadays, the shift from the bare-bones experience I remembered from a decade ago in high school gym class amazed me.

I decided to go simple for my first run, tapping in with my Apple Watch and committing to a 30-minute easy effort with just a podcast to entertain me.

The run itself was good, but left me puzzled. I immediately focused on how each foot strike offered a different sensation than I was used to outside. After a minute of adjusting the belt speed, I settled into a pace that felt similar to my outdoor easy runs. What I found, though, was that the treadmill speed read a completely different pace than my outdoor runs.

After 30 minutes at zero incline, I completed just 2.56 miles at an 11:51 pace with my heart rate right at my usual 150 beats per minute (bpm). That 11:51 average was nearly two minutes slower than my outdoor 10:00 easy pace, but I felt like I was right at my normal outdoor effort level.

Still, I walked away encouraged. I logged a run, avoided the weather, and felt great doing it.

My experiment continued with more 30-minute easy runs over the next couple of weeks. Each one raised the same question: Why did an effort that felt identical to my normal 10:00 outdoor easy runs translate to a treadmill pace of well over 11:00 per mile? Adding to the confusion, I got a new watch (the Coros Pace 4), and it consistently recorded slightly longer distances than the treadmill itself displayed.

After my third run, I brought all my questions to a chat with Birmingham-based RRCA level II- and USATF-certified run coach Alex Morrow, founder of Resolute Running. I described to him how, on the treadmill, I felt I was giving a similar effort compared with my outdoor runs, but was running at a significantly slower pace, and I asked him why he thought this was the case.

“When you’re outside and you’re running at an easy pace, you’re looking at the trees, you’re waving at other runners, and your mind gets to dissociate from what you’re doing,” Morrow says. “When you’re on a treadmill, there’s very little stimulation,” beyond your body moving.

Because I’d been running exclusively outdoors since high school, I was used to looking around at the cars as they passed by, the birds in the air, and any number of distractions along my route. As soon as I hopped on the treadmill, though, none of that was there to capture my attention. Right away, I locked in on the difference in every step, and became consumed by how far off my pace ended up being from what I expected.

Changing a long-held belief is tough, especially when it’s rooted in identity. “It’s like turning a battleship around,” says Morrow. “It takes time and it’s never easy.” In my case, the belief that “real runners” don’t use treadmills stuck around for years.

Once I started running on one, though, I accepted it as a suitable tool for consistent running almost immediately. The hardest part of flipping my mindset wasn’t logging the miles or dealing with boredom, it was simply stepping onto the belt in the first place.

If you’re new to treadmill running, or have avoided it for the same reasons I did, my best advice is to try it with an open mind. Don’t worry if your pace looks slower than what you’re used to seeing outside. That mental hurdle of mine ended up not really mattering much. I let effort guide my runs, my podcasts entertain me, and I judge my success based on time on feet rather than actual miles.

My biggest takeaway from the experience was consistency. According to Morrow, that’s where treadmill running becomes one of the most powerful tools a runner can use, especially in the winter.

Through my trial efforts, I realized I wasn’t frustrated with the treadmill itself, I was simply focused on learning more about my running. Curiosity helped me keep a steady schedule, and in just a few weeks, I’d already run more in the winter than I had in years.

“Consistency is so much more important than having one killer workout,” Morrow explains. “I would much rather you have four or five average workouts than three killer workouts.” This idea counters how a lot of runners think about training, especially when motivation dips. It’s flashy to chase breakthrough days in perfect conditions, but you build fitness by stacking days together, even when the circumstances aren’t ideal.

For runners who live in areas heavily impacted by harsh winter weather, the treadmill is a saving grace. “Something is always better than nothing,” Morrow says. “Jogging three miles on a treadmill is better than skipping your workout completely because it’s cold outside.”

When weather threatens to derail a week of training, the opportunity that a treadmill provides becomes crucial to your development as a runner. “Consistency creates physiological adaptations in your body that allow you to reach your goals,” Morrow says. Those adaptations include a boost in aerobic fitness development, running economy, VO2 max, and lactate threshold, he continues. It’s adaptations like these that establish an excellent fitness base for marathon training.

Looking back on my career as a recreational runner, my biggest mistake wasn’t refusing to run on the treadmill; it was letting that ignorance cost me months of consistent running every year. Now, the excuses that held me back are gone. I’ve continued using the treadmill to not only knock out frequent easy runs but conquer the occasional interval workout or speed session.

#8696. Like Jess McClain, I Took Time Off From Running—and Came Back Stronger. These Signs Mean It’s Time to Step Away.

Plus, the benefits you’ll gain from a break.

They say distance makes the heart grow fonder, and that’s true for me with running. But by “distance,” I don’t mean bumping up my mileage or running farther. I mean taking time and space away from my sport during seasons when I feel burned out, lost, or simply exhausted.

Around this time last year, I went from lifting two to three days a week while training for my first marathon to stopping workouts completely and struggling to get off my couch. The second I crossed the finish line, all I wanted to do was let my running shoes collect dust, avoid my local trail, and avoid stepping foot in the gym for a while.

Professional distance runner and New York City Marathon runner-up Jess McClain previously told Runner’s World she felt similarly about six years ago. At that time, she consistently stopped hitting her paces in her workouts and decided to step back from running—a break that lasted about two years.

In my case, I wasn’t as decisive. For months, I resisted the idea that I needed to take a break.

I’d heard that a month is generally how long you need to recover from a marathon, so I told myself that’s when I would jump into winter base training. But every time I tried to get back out there, I got bored and I struggled to recover from my runs. I waited until summer for the urge to work out again, but it never really came back.

For a while, I felt like getting burned out was my fault, that I must have pushed too hard in training. Looking back now—and with help from an expert—I understand that my break was exactly what I needed to get back to my sport in a sustainable way.

My break from running lasted about nine months, and I came back feeling like the runner I had always been before. Plus, I raced one of my fastest half marathons as my comeback.

Below I offer the telltale signs it’s time for a break from running, what a “break” really means, and the benefits you can gain from stepping away from the sport for a while—even if it seems impossible to do so at first.

The farther away I got from my training cycle, the more I realized how much I overtrained. I’d been strength training for 90 minutes three times a week with heavy weights while balancing 30-plus-mile weeks and 20-mile long runs. As I gained more perspective after my race ended, I noticed signs that I was in desperate need of a break.

“Pay attention to trends and patterns [throughout your training],” Erin Ayala, PhD, a sports psychologist, certified mental performance consultant, and founder of Skadi Sport Psychology, tells Runner’s World. “We all have bad days where the numbers aren’t coming together or a run feels harder than it normally does at a given pace. But if it continues to occur, then it can definitely be a sign to take a break,” she says.

Ayala says there are three main factors that often lead to athletic burnout. Here’s what each can look like, and how I experienced them.

You might need to take a step back if you find yourself hitting training plateaus despite putting in your best efforts.

I picked a training plan that included paces far too fast for my fitness level at the time, so every interval workout I did felt difficult, and my paces never really improved. The longer the intervals got, the farther I was from my desired split. But I kept checking off the weekly workouts anyway.

This lack of personal achievement and growth can halt your motivation levels. “When you’re not able to progress and you lose sight of [personal achievements] you’re just going through the motions, that’s a really big red flag,” Ayala says.

After the first month or so, marathon training started to feel more like a chore and I felt really tired and disconnected during my workouts. I figured it was probably normal because I had never run a marathon before, but it turns out that’s not how you should expect to feel daily in your training. “If the workouts are just a grind and you’re having to peel yourself off of the couch in order to get them in, and that’s a sustained pattern, then that’s another big red flag,” Ayala says.

A change in my relationship with running and my “why” meant grappling with my identity as a runner, which Ayala says is the third factor that can contribute to athletic burnout. You might ask yourself questions like, “Why do I even do this anymore?” and “What’s the point?” She says that if those questions linger for more than a week or so, then that’s a sign you might need a break.

By the time I got to the start line, I questioned why I was even there, and all I could do was get through it. “There’s a very real sense of grief and loss, and that’s really scary,” when taking a step back from running, Ayala explains. “Often we hang on quite desperately to our athletic identity when it’s also okay to move on and to do something different.”

Once I knew I needed a break from running, I didn’t quite know how to hit pause.

Then Ayala pointed out that perfectionism can affect your relationship with your sport. And simply hearing that helped me realize why I needed to step away.

There are two types of perfectionists, Ayala explains. The first type is the high achiever, who wants to be the best and perform at the top as much as possible. The second type of perfectionist takes a more “maladaptive form.” These individuals are highly motivated by others’ perceptions and expectations, she says. They might fear failure and generally don’t want to disappoint people.

That second type of perfectionism resonated with me because I realized I was listening to a nagging voice in my head that expected me to give absolutely everything I had to my training. And if I didn’t, I would face that critical voice’s judgment and let it fill me with disappointment and shame.

“Breaks can be helpful because they essentially force you to turn that perfectionistic tendency off. They’re a good way to keep yourself balanced,” Ayala adds.

Once I knew this and decided to take a break, I figured out how to fill my time.

Those first few months after marathon training, I was so excited to not think about running at all. Instead, I looked forward to filling my free time by rebooting my old Webkinz account (an online virtual-pet game popular in the mid-2000s), decorating my new apartment, and watching a lot of TV.

“First, just give yourself time. Then, you can create other bite-sized goals like daily movement, getting outside, spending time with friends, or exploring different hobbies,” Ayala suggests.

When I passed the two-month mark of my break, I took up pottery classes. While that hobby didn’t last, it gave me the space I needed from running.

I knew, deep down, that rest was probably what I needed. But when I took time off, I felt too anxious and ashamed to even enjoy it: I kept thinking about how much time I was wasting and how out-of-shape I felt. “The problem [with athletic burnout] isn’t that you just need to motivate yourself harder. You need to rest in order to get that intrinsic motivation back,” Ayala says.

Ayala explains that if we lose our intrinsic motivation, we often rely on feelings of shame and discipline to keep up with our routine, which ultimately isn’t sustainable.

When I was honest with myself, I found my new “why” for running—my intrinsic motivator—and that was because of how strong, creative, and capable it makes me feel.

One piece of advice from Ayala especially resonates with me: Accept where you’re at and normalize taking a break. “I would argue that getting burned out is a very normal and expected part of being an athlete,” she says. “If you are an athlete long enough, you are going to get burned out at some point and that’s okay. It doesn’t mean that you’re doing something wrong.”

Once I accepted that I was dealing with a longer-term case of burnout and some depression, I began to see light at the end of the tunnel. I set bite-sized goals, per Ayala’s suggestion, and began by committing to running just five minutes a day for a month. With that, running clicked for me again.

Looking back on my time away from running, I don’t view it with shame or anxiety anymore. I see it as both a period of my life when I learned about myself as an athlete and about how my brain works. It was also a time of physiological and mental recovery from so much training stress.

By stepping away, I unlocked a new life experience that can help inform me if—and probably when—I experience burnout again. That perspective shift alone lifts so much weight off my shoulders.

Plus, I’ve come back to the sport now feeling refreshed. I ran one of my fastest half marathons and feel ready to tackle another training plan. I have the drive to set and achieve goals again. And that’s an irreplaceable benefit to taking some time away.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.
